paras: The threatened lynching of Edward Green took place in Bronxville, New York, in November 1903, when residents threatened to lynch Green, a Black man of Mount Vernon, after he was identified as the man who had attacked the private secretary of former state senator Isaac N. Mills. Officials guarded Green, and two days after his arrest he was acquitted on the alibi testimony of a former mayor of Mount Vernon. Wire reports carried the story nationally, first as a jail guarded against lynchers and then as the narrow escape of an innocent man.

On November 10 the New York Evening World reported that a secretary of Mills had been attacked by a Black man in woods at Bronxville the previous Saturday night and had fought him off with her hatpin. That paper named her Miss Elsie Emory; later reports called her Miss Lillian Imrie or Miss Tilden Imrie. It added that a Black suspect had been released for want of identification and that "many citizens talk of organizing a vigilance committee."

According to the New-York Tribune, the assailant seized her by the throat near the Old Dutch Reformed Church, let go after she jabbed him with her hatpin, and fled when Clarence Moore came to her aid. A vigilance committee of Bronxville residents searched the woods, by the Evening World's account without result. Green, 28, called by the Tribune "the colored Berry Wall" of Mount Vernon, was arrested on Wednesday, November 11, charged with assault in the first degree after Miss Imrie identified him.

That night Judge Thatcher arraigned him privately in Police Chief Van Buren's parlor, where he pleaded not guilty and was held in $2,000 bail. Officials feared that friends of Miss Imrie might attack him, and the Tribune wrote that some villagers favored "taking the law into their own hands and lynching Green." The Associated Press reported that residents "became furious and threats of mob violence were freely made." Judging the Bronxville lockup unsafe, Judge Thatcher had Green held at Mount Vernon police headquarters.
Green denied the charge and said he had spent the evening on political errands in Port Chester and at Mayor Fiske's. His counsel claimed fifty alibi witnesses; Miss Imrie said she was positive.

On the night of November 13 Green was acquitted at Bronxville on the testimony of ex-Mayor Edwin W. Fiske, Mrs. Fiske and Stephen Van Tassell. A wire report said the Fiskes placed Green at their house at the hour of the assault. The Tribune wrote that the citizens were now "thankful that they waited until the case was tried." No report of charges against anyone who threatened Green appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press dispatch of November 12 ran from Butte and Salt Lake City to Providence, San Antonio, Montgomery and Worcester. Most headlines dwelt on the hatpin, such as "The Defensive Hatpin" and "Hatpin Saves Her Honor," and the Providence News stated before any trial that Green had "Foleniously Assaulted" the woman. The Montgomery Advertiser instead headed it "New York's Lynch Spirit."

The New York papers dwelt on Green himself, the Tribune listing his convictions and the Evening World headlining his claim that a black cat brought him bad luck. After the acquittal a second wire ran as "He Proved a Clean Alibi"; it alone called the complainant "a young white woman" and the charge attempted robbery and assault. The Deseret Evening News wrote in an editorial that the "lynching of an innocent negro was narrowly averted" and warned of men "sacrificed to the mob's fury" on false identification.
All the coverage found came from white newspapers; no Black newspaper account was found.

The Associated Press said a posse caught Green after a long chase and guarded him in the Bronxville jail; the closer New York papers said he was moved to Mount Vernon and mentioned no chase. Accounts of the attack differ on its hour and ending, and the Evening World later placed it "the night before election." The Deseret editorial placed the episode at Mount Vernon and claimed "the mob was for hanging him," which the news reports, describing threats only, do not show.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Edward Green
bases: Bronxville residents threatened to lynch Green, a Black man held on an assault charge, and officials guarded and moved him for that reason; no violence to him was reported, so this is a threatened lynching (A3, A5, A12).

Green was not killed or harmed: he was guarded, tried and acquitted (A5, A12, A16). The threats came from residents of Bronxville angered by an assault charge, a pretext of justice, but no number is given and no mob is reported to have gathered (A3, A5).

The AP dispatch and two New York papers, the Tribune and the Evening World, separately report the lynching threats and the precautions taken to protect Green (A3, A5, A6), and the Tribune and a separate wire both report his acquittal (A12, A16).

accounts.label: AP wire (first report)
accounts.gist: Green, 'notorious in Mount Vernon', was caught by a posse after a long chase; residents were furious and threatened mob violence; special guards protected him in the Bronxville jail.

accounts.label: New York local papers
accounts.gist: Green was arrested after Miss Imrie identified him, arraigned privately, and moved to Mount Vernon because officials feared Bronxville villagers or her friends would lynch him; he claimed an alibi.

accounts.label: Acquittal reports
accounts.gist: Green was acquitted on the testimony of ex-Mayor Fiske and others that he was at Fiske's house; Bronxville citizens were said to be thankful they had waited.

accounts.label: Deseret News editorial
accounts.gist: A mob 'was for hanging him' but consented to a trial; his acquittal showed how innocent men were lynched on false identification.

framing.detail: The AP dispatch ran under headlines stressing the hatpin and the assault ('The Defensive Hatpin', 'Hatpin Saves Her Honor', 'Negro Assaulted Young Woman'); Providence said he 'Foleniously Assaulted' her before any trial.
The Montgomery Advertiser headed the same dispatch 'New York's Lynch Spirit'.
The New York papers reported the threats and his alibi while calling him 'the colored Berry Wall', listing fourteen convictions, and mocking his 'black cat' hoodoo.
The Deseret News editorial called it a narrowly averted 'lynching of an innocent negro' and warned of false identification.
The acquittal wire ran as 'He Proved a Clean Alibi' with the subhead that Bronxville was 'Glad They Didn't Lynch Edward Green'.

info: Alleged attack on Saturday evening, November 7, 1903; Green arrested and threatened with lynching on Wednesday, November 11; acquitted on the night of Friday, November 13.
Bronxville, N.Y. (alleged attack near the Old Dutch Reformed Church; threats by Bronxville residents); Green held at the Mount Vernon police station.
Edward ('Ned') Green, a Black man of Mount Vernon, aged 28, the target of the lynching threats; not harmed.

Accused of seizing by the throat and attacking a young woman, private secretary to ex-Senator Isaac N. Mills; charged with assault in the first degree (Tribune); the acquittal wire called it an attempt 'to rob and assault'.
Unnamed residents of Bronxville ('citizens of Bronxville'; 'some Bronxville villagers'); officials also feared 'friends of Miss Imrie'.
